summary: NASA FIRMS Harmonization Platform is a web application for monitoring and analyzing active-fire hotspots detected by MODIS and VIIRS satellites. It standardizes and matches observations to reduce duplicate detections, then presents NASA FIRMS data through an interactive map and a historical fire-activity calendar. The application uses MODIS land-cover data to identify hotspots in vegetated areas. It also displays experimental 6-, 12-, and 24-hour indices for fire-persistence conditions and potential spread to nearby grid cells based on weather forecasts. These indices are not yet validated predictions; verified fire outcomes and time-stamped perimeters are needed before a predictive model can be deployed.
details:
Global Multi-Sensor Active-Fire Harmonization is a web application that brings MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations into a consistent view. It retrieves recent detections from NASA FIRMS, standardizes records from different sensors, and compares their locations and acquisition times to group related observations and reduce duplicate counts. Users can explore the results through an interactive map, filters, and a historical fire-activity calendar.

The application uses MODIS LC_Type1 land-cover data to identify hotspots in vegetated areas. It marks locations without raster coverage as unknown. An experimental map layer combines hourly weather forecasts with vegetation data to shade nearby grid cells by a relative spread index at 6, 12, and 24 hours. This is a conditional scenario if a fire remains active, not a validated probability or confirmed fire perimeter.

The project makes satellite fire records easier to compare across locations and dates. It is intended to help researchers, land managers, and monitoring teams examine historical patterns and identify periods that warrant closer attention.

We developed it with a Python backend, a React and TypeScript frontend, interactive mapping libraries, NASA FIRMS data, MODIS land-cover rasters, and hourly weather forecasts. We considered sensor differences, duplicate detections, observation gaps, incomplete raster coverage, and the limits of weather-based scenarios. A predictive model has not been deployed because verified fire outcomes and time-stamped perimeter data are still needed for training and evaluation.
